info.name: 2 · MBA Workshop — Advanced (ElecStore)
info.description:
# Meta Business Agent (MBA) — Advanced track

Everything the Basic track deliberately left out. **Run the Basic collection
first** — this one assumes `AGENT_ID`, `CONNECTOR_ID` and the eight core tools
already exist, and it shares the same environment.

## What is in here

| Folder | What it adds |
|---|---|
| 1 · Extra knowledge | `websites` (crawl) and `files` (upload) |
| 2 · The rest of the store | The other 18 tools — the whole purchase journey plus everything after it |
| 3 · Run without the agent | Execute a tool directly; the phone-macro proof |
| 4 · Skills | 5 journey skills (cart → changes) + 8 electronics behaviours |
| 5 · Connector lifecycle | Key rotation, OAuth, mTLS, update, error logs, delete |
| 6 · Proactive messaging | Agent Events — your API messages the customer first |
| 7 · Agent Eval | Cases, runs, summaries, per-conversation detail |
| 8 · Observability | Conversation turns — every step the agent took, for one consumer |
| 9 · Thread control | Take, pass to a role, release |
| 10 · Teardown | Remove what the workshop created |

## Suggested order

Folders 2 → 4 → 3 first: register the journey tools, upload the journey skills,
then prove them with `run` before a customer ever touches them. After that the
folders are independent — 6 (Agent Events) is the one worth doing next, because
it is the capability that changes the channel rather than extending it.

## The three shapes of a "real" integration

The Basic track builds the first shape only. The other two are what separates a
demo from a deployment:

1. **Pull** — the agent calls your API. Connector + tools. (Basic.)
2. **Push** — your API calls the agent. Agent Events, folder 6. This is what
   turns "where is my order?" into "your order is out for delivery", and it
   changes the economics of the channel more than any tool does.
3. **Prove** — Eval and Observability, folders 7 and 8. Scored eval runs and
   per-turn step traces are how you answer "is it actually working" without reading
   conversations one by one.

## Deliberately not exposed as tools

Four store endpoints have no agent tool, and that is a decision rather than an
oversight:

| Endpoint | Why no tool |
|---|---|
| `POST /v1/payments/{id}/simulate` | a test lever for humans, not an action an agent takes mid-conversation |
| `POST /v1/payments/{id}/refund` | money leaving the business should be a human decision |
| `POST /v1/shipments/{id}/advance` | fast-forwarding a delivery is a demo lever, not something to do to a real order |
| `GET /v1/events` | operator/debug feed, not a conversational capability |

An endpoint the agent cannot reach is invisible in a way an error is not — so
leaving one out has to be written down.

This collection calls **Meta APIs only**. Driving the store directly — settling a
payment, advancing a shipment — is done from the store's own API or its `/admin`,
and is deliberately out of scope here.

item.name: 01 · Knowledge beyond FAQs
item.description: FAQs and business info cover the answers you can enumerate. These three cover the ones you cannot.

request.description:
Adds pages of the business site as supplementary knowledge.

Fields: `url` (required), `crawl_depth` (default 1), `crawl_frequency` (daily/weekly/monthly/once), `include_patterns`, `exclude_patterns`, `metadata`. The response carries `crawl_status` (pending / in_progress / completed / failed) and `pages_crawled`.

**Exclude the transactional paths.** Crawling `/cart` and `/checkout` teaches the agent about a web checkout it cannot drive, and it will start sending people there instead of using the connector.

Also `GET` (list), `GET /{website_id}`, `PUT /{website_id}`, `DELETE /{website_id}`.

body.raw:
{
  "url": "https://elecstore.com",
  "crawl_depth": 2,
  "crawl_frequency": "weekly",
  "include_patterns": [
    "/products",
    "/warranty",
    "/delivery",
    "/blog"
  ],
  "exclude_patterns": [
    "/cart",
    "/checkout",
    "/account"
  ]
}

item.name: 01.03 · Upload a file (spec sheet / warranty PDF)

request.description:
Multipart, not JSON — do not set `Content-Type` by hand, Postman sets the boundary.

Good candidates for an electronics store: the warranty terms, a spec sheet per product family, the returns policy. Bad candidate: a price list — prices belong in the tools, where they cannot go stale.

Pick a file in the **Body → form-data** tab before sending.

Also `GET` (list and by id), `DELETE /{file_id}`.

item.name: 02 · The rest of the store
item.description:
The Basic track registers three tools, because product discovery is what three tools buy you. These eighteen complete the surface — the whole purchase journey plus everything after it.

Add them **one conversation at a time**. Every tool you add competes for the agent's attention; a connector with 21 tools picks worse on the eight that matter than a connector with eight.

Suggested order of value for an electronics store — this is also the shortest path to a complete purchase:

1. `create_cart` + `add_cart_item` + `get_cart` — a basket exists.
2. `create_checkout` + `complete_checkout` — an order exists.
3. `create_payment` + `get_payment` — it can be paid.
4. `find_my_orders` — "where is my order?", answered with zero back-and-forth.
5. `get_shipping_rates` + `select_shipping`, then `find_customer` + `create_customer`, then `get_order` + `track_shipment`, then `apply_discount` and `cancel_order`.

Stop after step 4 and you have a store that sells. Everything past it is polish.

request.description:
`POST /v1/customers` on the store API.

Create (or fetch) the customer record for the person you are chatting with. Their phone number is filled in automatically — never ask for it and never pass it yourself. Call this once before create_checkout so the order is linked to them. Returns the same customer if one already exists.

Reminders that cost a debugging session:
- Never declare `X-API-Key` as a tool header — the connector injects it, and declaring it again exposes the key to the agent as an input.
- Every `{placeholder}` in `path` needs exactly one matching key in `path_parameters`.
- Top-level input names must be unique across path, query, header and body.
- Nested object properties and array items are **JSON-string-wrapped**; top-level fields are plain objects.
- A field with a `binding` of `macro` is filled by the runtime and stripped from what the agent sees, so the model cannot hallucinate the phone number.

const v = j.id ?? j.data?.id ?? (Array.isArray(j.data) ? j.data[0]?.id : undefined);
else console.warn('toolId_create_customer not found in response — set it by hand');

request.description: Twenty-one tools, one per store operation the agent is allowed to reach — the three from the Basic track plus the eighteen here.

item.name: 03 · Run tools without the agent
item.description:
`run` executes a tool directly, bypassing the agent entirely. This splits **"my API is wrong"** from **"the agent chose wrong"**, which is almost always the question you actually have.

Do this before you blame a conversation. Reading a transcript to discover the connector had a stale API key is an expensive way to spend an afternoon.

request.description: `input` is a **stringified** JSON object — `{"input": "{\"q\":\"…\"}"}`, not a nested object. Getting this wrong returns a validation error that reads like a problem with your tool definition and is not.

Note what is **not** in `input`: the phone number. `find_my_orders` binds `phone` to the `WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER` macro, so the runtime fills it and the field is stripped from the schema the agent sees — the model cannot hallucinate or misquote it.

This is the highest-value line in the whole integration: "where is my order?" resolves with zero back-and-forth, and it costs one `binding` clause.

Available macros are `WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER`, `WHATSAPP_IDENTITY_HASH` and `WHATSAPP_CURRENT_STATUS_ID`. `binding` also takes `{"kind":"default","value":"…"}` for constants the agent should not supply. Bindings work on **scalar fields only** — never on an object, an array, or inside array items.

Outside a real conversation the macro has nothing to resolve, so an empty result here is expected — what you are checking is that the call is accepted.
Which tool is failing, how often, and how slow. Errors take roughly ten minutes to appear and are retained for seven days, so an empty result right after a failure is normal rather than reassuring.

item.name: 04 · Skills — the purchase journey and beyond
item.description:
Thirteen skills. The first five complete the purchase journey the Basic track stops short of — cart, checkout, payment, order status, cancellations. The other eight are the electronics-specific behaviours: accessory attach, spec comparison, stock-outs, warranty and RMA, Brazilian payment expectations, entry-point context from ads and marketing messages, proactive events, and tool-error handling.

**Upload the journey skills only once their tools exist** (folder 2). A skill naming a tool that is not registered is the most confusing failure on this surface: the agent neither errors nor complies, it quietly does something else.

Each skill says up front when it applies, when it does not, and which skill takes over next — two skills claiming the same moment produce duplicate replies.

Upload them a few at a time and test in between. Adding thirteen at once leaves you no way to tell which one changed the behaviour.

1. Read the event description. It is written for you, not for the customer - do not

{

  "description": "Use whenever a connector tool returns an error, times out, or returns something you cannot parse.",
  "skill": "# Tool errors - one retry, then say something true

APPLIES the moment a tool call returns a non-success response or nothing at all.
DOES NOT APPLY to a successful response that simply contains no results - an empty
search is a discovery problem, not an error.

## What to do, by kind
- **401 / 403** - the store connection is misconfigured. Do not retry, do not
  explain the credential problem to the customer. Say you cannot reach the store
  right now and hand off.
- **404** - the id you used does not exist. Check whether you passed a product id
  where a variant id was needed, or a stale cart id. Re-read the id from the last
  response and try once. If it fails again, start that step over rather than
  guessing.
- **409 conflict** - this is information, not a failure. Stock conflicts, an already
  shipped order, an already completed checkout. Read what the response says and act
  on it; see the stock-and-alternatives and changes skills.
- **422 / 400 validation** - you sent something malformed. Read which field the
  response names, fix that field, and retry once.
- **429** - too many calls. Wait, then retry once. Do not fan out more calls.
- **500 / 503 / timeout** - the store is unhealthy. Retry **once**. If it fails
  again, say the store system is temporarily unavailable and hand off.

## Rules
- **One retry maximum, per step.** A second failure of the same tool for the same
  request is a handoff, always.
- Never show the customer a status code, a stack trace, a request id or a raw error
  body.
- Never say "please try again later" and stop. Either retry yourself, or hand off.
- Never invent the data the failed call would have returned. An unavailable price is
  unknown, not estimated.
- If a write may have partially succeeded - complete_checkout, create_payment - read
  it back with get_order or get_payment before telling the customer anything. Never
  blind-retry a write.
- Tell the customer what you are doing in plain language: "One moment, let me try
  de novo" is fine; silence for eight seconds is not."
}

item.name: 06 · Proactive messaging — Agent Events
item.description:
Connectors let the agent **pull** from your API. The Agent Event API lets your API **push** to the agent, so it messages the customer first — "your PIX has been confirmed", "your order is out for delivery" — without them asking.

```
POST /{entity_id}/agent_event      X-API-Version: 1.0.0
{ "to": "5511999998888",
  "event": { "type": "...", "description": "...", "payload": "{...}" } }
→ 200 { "status": "accepted", "id": "..." }
```

## Three things that are easy to get wrong

- **`to` is bare digits — no leading `+`**, despite being a phone number.
- **`event.payload` is a JSON-encoded string**, not a nested object.
- **`event.description` is what the agent reads** to decide what to say. It is a prompt, not a log line. `description` caps at 1024 characters, `payload` at 4096.

`accepted` means enqueued, not delivered. Delivery is asynchronous and Cloud API can still reject the outbound message — an expired 24-hour window, an invalid thread. Poll `GET /{entity_id}/agent_event/{id}` for processing status.

Every request in this folder is a Meta API call. To make a *real* event happen rather than hand-crafting one, drive the store from its own API or its `/admin` — settle a payment, advance a shipment — and let it push the event itself.

The `proactive-events` skill (3.10) is what teaches the agent to send exactly one message and not to re-verify with a tool.

item.name: 08 · Observability — conversation turns
item.description:
One endpoint, and it answers the question you actually have when a conversation went wrong: **what did the agent do, step by step?**

```
GET /{entity_id}/insights/conversations/turns?user_phone_number=…
```

A *turn* is one exchange: the customer message, and everything the agent did in response. Each turn carries a `turn_id`, an optional `e2e_latency_ms`, and an ordered list of `steps` — which is where you see the tool calls, in order, with what went in and what came back.

## Why this beats reading a transcript

A transcript tells you what the customer saw. The steps tell you why. The two diagnoses it separates are the two you cannot tell apart from the chat alone:

- **The agent never called the tool.** A tool description problem, or too many tools competing. Fix the description, or delete a tool.
- **The agent called it and ignored or misread the result.** A skill problem. Fix the instruction that governs that stage.

Both look identical as "the bot gave a wrong price".

## What it is not

It is scoped to **one consumer at a time** — `user_phone_number` is required, and there is no fleet-wide view here. This is a debugging endpoint, not an analytics dashboard. For "is the agent good in aggregate", use the eval runs in folder 6.

request.description:
The whole reconstructed conversation with this consumer, newest turns included, as an ordered list of turns and the steps inside each.

## Parameters

| Param | Notes |
|---|---|
| `user_phone_number` | **Required.** The consumer, in E.164. |
| `limit` | 1–100. Anything outside that range is a 400, including `0`. |
| `after` | Cursor for the next page. |

## Reading the response

- `turn_id` — stable, and it is what the cursor is keyed on, so a turn arriving mid-pagination cannot shift your page the way an offset would.
- `e2e_latency_ms` — optional. When a customer says "it took forever", this is the number, not your impression of the number.
- `steps` — ordered. Read them as a sequence: this is the agent reasoning, calling a tool, reading the result, and deciding what to say.

## Errors worth recognising

- **401** — token problem. Same token as the rest of this collection.
- **400** — missing or malformed `user_phone_number`, or a `limit` outside 1–100.
- **405** — you sent POST. This endpoint is GET only.
- **404 with an unknown API version** — check the `X-API-Version` header.

**Known limitation:** two records can share a `turn_id`. With `limit=1`, both get the same cursor, so following `after` can return the same record indefinitely. Use a realistic `limit` (10–25) and you will not meet it.

item.name: 08.02 · Narrow to a time window, and page through

request.description:
The same endpoint, scoped to when the thing you are debugging actually happened. On a chatty number the unfiltered call is mostly noise.

| Param | Notes |
|---|---|
| `start_timestamp_ms` | Inclusive lower bound. |
| `end_timestamp_ms` | Inclusive upper bound. |

Three things about these bounds that are easy to get wrong:

- **They are milliseconds.** Passing seconds is not an error — it silently matches nothing, which reads exactly like "there were no conversations".
- **They filter on the *start* of the turn**, taken from the timestamp of the customer's message. A turn that began inside the window and ran past the end is included whole.
- **An inverted range is a 400**, not an empty result: `end_timestamp_ms must be greater than or equal to start_timestamp_ms`. Equal bounds are legal and return the turn at that instant.

Set `TURNS_START_MS` and `TURNS_END_MS` in the environment. Filtering composes with `limit` and with cursor pagination, so you can narrow first and page second.

Supplying both `before` and `after` is a 400. When you reach the end of the results, the response simply omits `after` — that absence is the terminator, not an empty string.

item.name: 09 · Thread control
item.description:
The agent is not the only participant in a conversation. Thread control decides who owns it.

```
POST /business/whatsapp/phone_numbers/{phone_number_id}/thread_control
```

## Three actions

| Action | Called by | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `take` | an app authorised to escalate | the caller becomes the owner |
| `pass` | the current owner | ownership moves to the role you name |
| `release` | the current owner | ownership returns to the default, silently |

They are not symmetric, and the asymmetry is where integrations go wrong:

- **Only the current owner can `pass` or `release`.** If the agent holds the conversation, take it first.
- **`take` may be restricted.** Whether your app is allowed to take a conversation depends on the phone number's routing configuration, not on your token. A rejection here is configuration, not a malformed request.
- **`metadata` is free text, max 2000 characters**, carried along with the transfer. Write something a person debugging the other side would want to read.

Note the host and the path: `api.facebook.com/business/whatsapp/phone_numbers/{phone_number_id}/thread_control`. It is **not** a Graph edge — `graph.facebook.com/v23.0/{id}/thread_control` answers `Unknown path components` on v23, v24 and v25, while this path answers an auth error. Both checked live.

request.description:
Takes ownership of the conversation from whoever holds it, **without having to send a message first**. That last part is the point: it lets you mute the agent while a person is still composing a reply, rather than the agent answering over the top of them.

If your app is not authorised to take conversations on this phone number, this is rejected. That is the number's routing configuration, not your request.

item.name: 09.02 · Pass the thread back to the agent

request.description:
The difference between `pass` and `release`:

- **`release`** drops the conversation back to the default owner and names nobody. Use it when the conversation is genuinely finished.
- **`pass`** hands it to a **named role**. Use it when the conversation is not finished and you know who should continue it — here, the AI agent.

## The shape that trips people up

`target_role` is **nested inside a `control_pass` object**, not flat on the body:

```json
{ "control_pass": { "target_role": "ai_agent" } }
```

Sending `action: "pass"` with no `control_pass` object is a 400.

This is the natural bookend to 8.1: take the conversation for a person, and pass it back when they are done. Skipping the pass leaves the agent silent on that number for that customer, which looks exactly like the agent being broken.

Give up ownership without naming a successor — it returns to the default owner silently.

Use `release` when the work is done and `pass` (8.2) when someone specific should continue. Releasing when you meant to pass is how conversations end up unattended.
